Hi! I'm Rohith Raj, a student interested in technology, coding, innovation, and fire safety. I've worked on projects like a harmful gas detector and a fire engine robot.

Our team, Agni Rakshakar 🔥, aims to develop innovative solutions for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. I'm looking for teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, web development, data analysis, design, and research. Enthusiasm, creativity, and teamwork are always welcome.

Let's learn, innovate, and build something amazing together
summary:
FLARE-X is an AI-powered scientific discovery platform that analyses microgravity combustion research to find hidden patterns in how fire behaves in space. Instead of only displaying existing results, it harmonises experiment data, learns how conditions such as oxygen level and airflow relate to flame behaviour, and flags anomalies, meaning results that deviate from what similar experiments predict. It also maps research gaps in the tested parameter space and recommends the next experiments with the highest expected information gain.

We built a working prototype with an anomaly explorer, a gap map, an experiment recommender, and a natural-language “ask the data” tool. It currently runs on synthetic demo data and is designed to ingest NASA’s real combustion datasets.

This addresses the challenge by turning scattered data into actionable fire-safety insight. It matters because fire is a critical hazard on spacecraft and future Moon and Mars habitats, and experiment time is scarce. FLARE-X helps scientists get more from existing data and focus on the questions that matter most.
details: FLARE-X is an AI-powered discovery platform for microgravity combustion research. It follows four steps: ingest, learn, discover, recommend. Ingest: Combustion experiment data is harmonised into one schema (oxygen level, airflow, fuel or material, spread rate), with each record linked to its source. Learn: The platform estimates the flame behaviour expected under each set of conditions, based on similar experiments. Discover: Experiments that deviate strongly from that expectation are flagged as anomalies and ranked by novelty. Examples are flames that persist at oxygen levels where similar runs burn slowly, or flames that are unexpectedly suppressed. Recommend: A gap map shows which oxygen × airflow regions have little or no data. The recommender ranks the next experiments by sparse coverage, closeness to anomalies, and relevance to crewed-cabin atmospheres. The prototype has four views: an anomaly explorer, a research gap map, a recommended-experiments list, and an “ask the data” search. It currently runs on synthetic demo data that imitates microgravity flame-spread experiments. The analysis pipeline runs live in the browser and is built to accept NASA combustion datasets, such as those in the Physical Sciences Informatics repository. Benefits and intended impact Scientists get more from existing data and can find non-obvious patterns faster. Limited ISS and drop-tower time goes to the experiments most likely to answer open questions. Fire-safety engineers get a clearer picture of which conditions are well understood and which are not. This matters for spacecraft and future Moon and Mars habitats. Findings about flames without buoyancy can also improve combustion models on Earth. Tools and technologies The prototype is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG charts and no external libraries. The anomaly detection (neighbour-based expectation with residual scoring), gap mapping and recommendation scoring are implemented in JavaScript. The demo deck was made with Claude. Planned for the full version: Python (pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch), Isolation Forest or autoencoders for anomaly detection, SHAP for explainability, Bayesian optimisation for experiment suggestions, and an LLM layer for extracting data from papers and answering questions. No special hardware is required. Creativity Most research tools only display data. FLARE-X is built to generate hypotheses: it points to what looks unusual, shows what has never been tested, and suggests what to run next. Combining anomaly discovery, gap mapping and experiment recommendation in one loop is the core idea. Factors considered Scientific honesty: An anomaly is a hypothesis, not a finding. The platform reports confidence, links each result to its source, and is designed for expert review. Small datasets: Microgravity combustion data is limited, so models can be uncertain and should not be over-trusted. Data quality: Combining datasets with different formats and units can introduce errors, so provenance and spot checks are built in. Transparency: The prototype uses synthetic data, and we state this clearly so no demo result is mistaken for a real discovery. Usability: Researchers and safety engineers can explore the data without writing code.
